title: Recursive Formulas
short: Define a sequence by its first term and a rule for the next.
trouble: Students mix up aₙ and aₙ₊₁ when writing the rule.

blocks.html: In Algebra 1 you described Arithmetic Sequences and Geometric Sequences with explicit formulas, which jump straight to any term. A recursive formula describes the same sequences step by step instead: where to start, and how to get from one term to the next.

A recursive formula gives (1) the first term, such as $a_1 = 5$, and (2) a rule for each later term from the one before it, such as $a_n = a_{n-1} + 3$ for $n \ge 2$. Arithmetic: $a_n = a_{n-1} + d$. Geometric: $a_n = r \cdot a_{n-1}$.

Many processes are naturally described one step at a time: a savings account that earns interest and gets a deposit each month, $a_n = 1.01\,a_{n-1} + 50$, or a population that doubles every year. The recursive rule says exactly what happens in one step. The explicit formula is what you get after following the rule $n - 1$ times: adding $d$ that many times gives $a_1 + (n - 1)d$.

steps: Each time $n$ goes up by 1, $a_n$ goes up by 4.

blocks.title: Two previous terms
blocks.q: $a_1 = 1$, $a_2 = 1$ and $a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2}$. List the first 7 terms.
steps: Each term is the sum of the two before it: $1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13$.

blocks.html: Mixing up $a_n$ and $a_{n+1}$. "$a_n = a_{n-1} + 3$" and "$a_{n+1} = a_n + 3$" say the same thing (each term is 3 more than the one before), but "$a_{n-1} = a_n + 3$" says each term is 3 less. Read it in words: "this term equals the previous term plus 3." Then check by computing $a_2$ from $a_1$.
